lessons.title: Passing lines
lessons.objective: Choose the passing line on the track.

payload.prompt: Where on the track can a pass happen? Tap the passing line.

diagram.alt: Overhead view of a race car turn with low, middle and high lanes marked.

regions.label: Low line
regions.feedback: The low line is often the fastest groove, so trailing cars dive low to make the pass.

regions.label: Middle
regions.feedback: The middle groove works when the low line is blocked or when a car has momentum.

regions.label: High line
regions.feedback: The high line can work late in a race if the car has momentum off the straightaway.

explanation.correct: All three lanes are used for passes depending on track, tires and traffic.

payload.prompt: When is the best time to execute a passing attempt?

options.text: In the middle of the straightaway when you have momentum.
On entry to the turn when you have gained a run from drafting.
Whenever the other driver makes a mistake.

explanation.correct: Right. A run off the draft sets up a pass into the turn, where the extra speed lets you dive to a better line.
explanation.incorrect: The best passing setup is a run off the draft into a turn. That extra speed (the 'run') lets you out-brake the leader and dive to the inside line.

payload.prompt: Can you pass up high on the track?

scene.alt: Bird's-eye view of a turn with two cars racing side-by-side on the high groove.

choices.label: Yes, the high groove works in certain situations.
No, you can only pass low.

explanation.correct: Yes. The high groove is slower but can work for a pass if your car has momentum or if rubber has built there.
explanation.incorrect: The high line is not the fast groove, but it can be used for a pass if conditions are right or if you have a run. Multi-groove racing is part of the sport.

payload.prompt: Match the groove to what happens there.

pairs.definition: The inside line; often the fastest lane where rubber has built grip.
The lane between low and high; used when low is blocked or when chasing.
The outside line; slower but sometimes available for a run or late-race pass.

distractorDefinitions: The pit road route to the stall.

explanation.summary: Three grooves offer three passing zones; the fast one changes as rubber builds and conditions shift.

payload.prompt: Most passes happen on the {{timing}} into a turn.
payload.template: Most passes happen on the {{timing}} into a turn.

explanation.correct: Right. Turn entry is where a run off drafting gives an overtaker the best shot.
explanation.incorrect: Most passes succeed on turn entry, where speed from a draft run lets the trailing car dive to the inside or stay wide. Exit is too late.

lessons.title: Restart lane and jump
lessons.objective: Pick the restart lane and gain spots off the jump.

configuration.prompt: Green flag restart: inside or outside lane? Choose and watch the lineup change.
configuration.setup: A caution brings the field down to restart. You are in the choose line and must pick: stay inside (safe, nose-to-tail position) or take the outside (risky, but can run faster if the lane has momentum). See how both lanes fan out and stack up on the restart.

payload.prompt: What is the restart?

options.text: When the race begins after a caution flag and cars line up in double file.
When a car's engine is restarted during a pit stop.
The moment the green flag waves, which is when all pit stops end.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A restart is the racing resumption after caution. Cars line up two abreast (double file) behind the leader and race resumes on the green flag.
explanation.incorrect: The restart is when racing resumes after a caution. The field is set in a double-file lineup, and the leader controls the restart moment. Restarts are where many passes happen.

payload.prompt: On a restart, does the leader choose which lane to take?

scene.alt: Diagram showing a restart lineup with two lanes, the leader ahead.

choices.label: No, the leader has no choice; the lanes are set.
Yes, the leader picks inside or outside first.

explanation.correct: Right. The choose rule means drivers in the running order choose left or right in sequence, starting behind the leader. The leader does not choose; the second-place car picks first.
explanation.incorrect: The choose rule is the strategy layer: drivers in running order pick their lane in sequence (inside or outside). The leader keeps their position; the second-place car chooses first.

payload.prompt: You are second on the restart. Inside or outside lane?

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: Second place, one car length behind the leader

facts.label: Tire age
facts.value: Both you and the leader have fresh tires (just pitted)

facts.label: Recent momentum
facts.value: The outside lane seemed stronger in practice

facts.label: Laps remaining
facts.value: 45 to go

options.label: Choose inside lane.
options.consequence: You line up nose-to-tail and can drive off the leader's bumper. Safe and predictable, but you are behind.
considerations: You stay close to the leader.
But no early advantage off the line.

options.label: Choose outside lane.
options.consequence: If the outside has run, you can jump the leader on acceleration and gain the lead into turn 1.
considerations: You can out-accelerate from the side.
High risk if you get blocked.

payload.expertNote: Lane choice is a judgment call based on track, practice runs and momentum. The best lane that day often rewards the brave.

lessons.title: Getting clean air
lessons.objective: Explain how to pass once you are out of dirty air.

payload.prompt: Can you pass without having clean air?

scene.alt: Diagram showing a follower car in dirty air trying to pass the leader.

choices.label: Yes, you can pass even in dirty air.
No, you must have clean air to pass.

explanation.correct: Yes, but it is much harder. Dirty air hurts your front grip, so a pass in dirty air requires ideal conditions or a big speed advantage.
explanation.incorrect: You can pass in dirty air if your car is faster or if you take advantage of a mistake, but dirty air makes passing very difficult. Most clean-air passes happen when the trailing car exits dirty air and has front grip.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: Once I got clean air, I had a shot.

options.text: Once I moved out of the turbulent air behind the leader, my car had grip to pass.
Once the weather cleared up, I could race harder.
Once the pit crew fixed the air vents in the car.

payload.translation: When I moved out of the disturbed air behind the leader, my car was fast enough to attempt a pass.

followUps.line: Clean air gives you front grip because no car is disrupting the airflow.
followUps.why: Aerodynamic effects decide whether a pass is even possible on downforce-sensitive tracks.

followUps.line: A clean-air pass often happens three-wide into a turn when the inside car clears the leader.
followUps.why: Once you have grip, you can turn better and dive to a different line.

payload.prompt: What does dirty air do to a following car?

options.text: It slows the engine by restricting intake airflow.
It reduces front grip, making the car pushy and hard to turn.
It creates a slipstream that speeds up the car.

explanation.correct: Right. Dirty air from the leader's wake reduces front grip and makes you push (understeer). That is why passing out of dirty air is so much easier.
explanation.incorrect: Dirty air is turbulent air behind another car. It disrupts the airflow over your splitter and nose, reducing downforce and front-end grip. The result: you push and cannot turn as well as the leader.

payload.prompt: A clean-air pass is easiest when {{condition}}.
payload.template: A clean-air pass is easiest when {{condition}}.

options: the trailing car gets out of dirty air
the leader makes a pit stop
gaps.correct: the trailing car gets out of dirty air

explanation.correct: Right. A trailing car exiting dirty air suddenly has grip. That is the moment to attack.
explanation.incorrect: A clean-air pass occurs when the trailing car moves from dirty air to clean air and gains front-end grip. That grip delta is what opens the passing window.

lessons.title: Blocking and being blocked
lessons.objective: Judge whether a block is legal.

payload.prompt: Is blocking a legal move in NASCAR?

scene.alt: Side-by-side view of two cars, one moving to block the other.

choices.label: Yes, a block is legal once per pass attempt.
No, blocking is always a penalty.

explanation.correct: Yes. One block per attempt is legal and expected; it is a racing move. Repeated blocks or late blocks anger rivals and can cost you later.
explanation.incorrect: Blocking is legal. A leading car can move once to defend a position. Multiple blocks, moving back and forth repeatedly, or a very late block may be penalized or draw retaliation.

payload.prompt: He moves to block, then you move again and he moves again. What do you do?

facts.label: Position
facts.value: You are third, trying to pass second

facts.label: The block
facts.value: He blocks low, you go high, he blocks high; back-and-forth blocking

facts.label: History with driver
facts.value: Neutral, no prior incidents

options.label: Accept the block and wait.
options.consequence: Respectable racing. You lose this battle but earn respect for clean driving.
considerations: You show respect for the fight.
But you might not get another shot.

options.label: Bump him slightly to upset his line.
options.consequence: A bump off his line is fair payback for repeated blocking. He loses momentum and you may dive past.
considerations: A small bump is within bounds.
It might be the only way past.

options.label: Wreck him to send a message.
options.consequence: A crash ends both of you and ruins your reputation. Not worth 8 laps for position.
considerations: You both DNF if it turns ugly.
Other drivers will remember a wreck.

payload.expertNote: Repeated blocking—moving back and forth—crosses the line from defense into aggression and invites a bump or payback.

payload.prompt: Match the block type to what it means.

pairs.definition: A single move to defend your line; legal and expected.
Moving back and forth to defend; can be penalized or provoke retaliation.
A block at the last moment when the overtaker is committed; often dirty and draws anger.

explanation.summary: One block is a racing move. Multiple blocks and late blocks are not and can earn a reputation for dirty driving.

payload.prompt: When is a block penalized?

options.text: Every time you move to defend your line.
When you repeatedly block back-and-forth or block very late into the corner.
Never; NASCAR allows unlimited blocks.

explanation.correct: Right. One block is clean racing. Multiple blocks or a very late block can be flagged by NASCAR if it is deemed unsafe or unsporting.
explanation.incorrect: Blocking is legal, but excessive blocking—moving multiple times or blocking so late that the overtaker cannot avoid contact—may draw a penalty flag. The line between racing and wrecking matters.

payload.prompt: Where is the braking zone? Tap the part of the track.

diagram.alt: Diagram of a road-course turn with approach, braking zone and apex marked.

regions.label: Straight approach
regions.feedback: You are at full throttle here; braking has not started.

regions.label: Braking zone
regions.feedback: The braking zone is where drivers slow down before the turn. A pass here is out-braking the leader.

regions.label: Apex (turn center)
regions.feedback: The apex is too late; the pass must happen on entry, in the braking zone.

explanation.correct: Passes on a road course often happen in the braking zone, where the trailing car out-brakes the leader and gains inside position.

payload.prompt: What is the key to passing on a road course?

options.text: Braking later than the car ahead and diving to the inside.
Drafting down the straightaway to build speed.
Having a higher top speed on the straights.

explanation.correct: Exactly. A road-course pass is about braking: out-brake the leader into a corner and you can take the inside line. Skill and patience win.
explanation.incorrect: Road-course racing is about braking precision. A trailing car can pass by braking later, diving to the inside of a corner and carrying more speed through the apex. Aggression in the braking zone is the move.

payload.prompt: You are faster in the braking zone. Do you dive for the inside?

facts.label: Current position
facts.value: Second place

facts.label: Skill
facts.value: You brake better than the leader

facts.label: Turn
facts.value: Tight 90-degree right hander

options.label: Dive inside in the braking zone.
options.consequence: Out-braking the leader gains you inside position. If you nail the turn, you are past. Road-course passing is about braking.
considerations: You have 20 laps for multiple attempts.

options.label: Wait for a mistake.
options.consequence: Conservative, but you might never get a cleaner shot. Patient driving keeps you safe but costs time.

payload.expertNote: Road-course specialists pass in the braking zone. Out-braking is how passes happen when driving skill is the separator.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: I out-braked him into the chicane.

options.text: I braked later and harder than he did, diving to the inside of the quick left-right section.
I used more brakes than he had installed.
I forced his brakes to fail.

payload.translation: I braked later than the leader, gaining inside position into the chicane (a quick left-right turn).

followUps.line: Out-braking means braking later than your competitor; it is the signature road-course pass.
followUps.why: On road courses, braking point is where passes are made, not on the straight or exit.

followUps.line: A failed out-braking attempt can result in a crash at the apex if you run out of room.
followUps.why: Road-course racecraft is about knowing the limit and executing perfectly; one tenth of a second too late and you are in the wall.

lessons.title: Lapped traffic
lessons.objective: Explain how lapped cars affect racing.

payload.prompt: You are fourth; a lapped car is in your way. Do you pass or wait?

facts.label: Your position
facts.value: Fourth, hunting third

facts.label: Lapped car
facts.value: Sixth place (one lap down) is slower and in your way

facts.label: Gap to third
facts.value: Half second back

options.label: Pass the lapped car and keep hunting.
options.consequence: Overtaking the lapped car costs you time but clears your line. You can now close on third.
considerations: The lapped car is just in the way.

options.label: Let the lapped car clear on its own.
options.consequence: The lapped car might yield on the next lap if it sees you are faster. You save fuel and tires.
considerations: The car behind you is losing time too.
But it could also stay in the way.

payload.expertNote: Lapped traffic is a hazard for leaders but a tool for anyone else; passing them or using them can change the race.

payload.prompt: What does 'a lap down' mean?

options.text: A car that has completed one fewer lap than the leader and is no longer in contention.
A car that is three seconds behind the leader.
A car that has pit stops remaining.

explanation.correct: Right. A lapped car has one full lap fewer than the leader. It is still racing but out of contention for the win.
explanation.incorrect: Being a lap down means the leader has lapped you—you are one full lap behind. You are still on track and racing, but you cannot win unless the leader crashes or pits late.

payload.prompt: Can lapped traffic help a chasing driver?

scene.alt: Diagram showing a leader slowing for lapped traffic while a chaser runs free.

choices.label: Yes, a lapped car can hold up the leader.
No, lapped traffic only hurts the chaser.

explanation.correct: Yes. A lapped car might slow the leader more than the chaser (if the chaser is smoother or faster), closing the gap.
explanation.incorrect: Lapped traffic is usually harder on the leader because a chaser can sometimes thread around better. Smart drivers use traffic to their advantage and close gaps.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: We got held up by traffic.

options.text: Slower, lapped cars blocked our path and cost us speed.
The pit crew was stuck and we waited in the stall.
Road construction delayed the race start.

payload.translation: We had to navigate around or slow for lapped cars in our way.

followUps.line: Lapped traffic is both a hazard and a factor; it can help or hurt depending on who is faster.
followUps.why: On a restart, lapped cars can shuffle the running order and give someone new a shot.

followUps.line: Free passes and wave-arounds are rules designed to manage when lapped cars cause too much disruption.
followUps.why: Letting a lapped car get back on the lead lap reduces frustration and keeps racing close.

statement.speaker: driver
statement.text: He will get some payback for that.

options.text: He will face retaliation on track in a future race or later in this race.
He will receive a financial refund.
He will be fined by NASCAR.

payload.translation: He will face retaliation or a bump if he crossed the line; it is part of the driver code.

followUps.line: Payback is a NASCAR tradition; if you wreck someone or block dirty, expect a bump later.
followUps.why: Drivers police themselves and each other on track. Respect and consequences shape behavior.

followUps.line: Payback does not mean a wreck; it can be a bump, blocking, or a bump-draft that takes a position.
followUps.why: There is a spectrum from clean racing to dirty; payback can stay within that spectrum.

payload.title: She expects payback
payload.setting: After a wreck caused by her driver's rival.

exchanges.theirMessage: He just wrecked my guy. Next race, he is getting a bump.

replies.text: Do you think that will settle it, or does it keep going?
replies.theirResponse: Depends on what the bump does. If it is clean, maybe it ends it.
replies.coachNote: You acknowledged payback tradition and asked if it ends the feud.

replies.theirResponse: It is, but I hope he understands.
replies.coachNote: Empathy is good, but ask a follow-up about the outcome.

replies.text: That is just how it is in NASCAR.
replies.theirResponse: Yeah, but nobody wants it to get out of hand.
replies.coachNote: True, but showing you get the stakes helps.

payload.closingNote: Payback is tradition, but drivers also know when to let it go.

payload.prompt: Is payback the same as a wreck?

scene.alt: Two-car contact diagram showing a bump vs a crash.

choices.label: No, payback can be clean contact or blocking.
Yes, payback always ends in a wreck.

explanation.correct: Right. Payback is retaliation, but it does not have to be a wreck. A bump, a block or a pass can be payback.
explanation.incorrect: Payback is the tradition of responding to a wrong, but it does not always mean wrecking. A bump that costs track position, a block, or beating someone fair-and-square can all be payback.

payload.prompt: He wrecked you last race. Today he is behind you. Do you wreck him back?

facts.label: What happened
facts.value: He dumped you last week at the end of the race

facts.label: Today
facts.value: He is in sixth, you are running fourth

facts.label: Points situation
facts.value: You are close in points; a DNF hurts

options.label: Race him clean and beat him fair.
options.consequence: You earn respect and keep racing. A clean win is better than a wreck. If he comes up the field, you can race him then.

options.label: Bump him off if he tries to pass.
options.consequence: Fair payback; you cost him track position without wrecking him. He gets the message.
considerations: But it does not guarantee he learns.

options.label: Wreck him like he wrecked you.
options.consequence: You might both DNF. Even if he DNFs and you survive, you are now the dirty driver. Reputation matters.
considerations: But you risk your race and your image.
Feuds escalate when you trade wrecks.

payload.expertNote: Payback is tradition, but wreck-for-wreck turns a one-time grudge into a feud. Smart racers respond with a bump or a clean beat, then move on.

lessons.title: Racing vs wrecking
lessons.objective: Judge whether contact is racing or wrecking.

payload.prompt: Is all contact in NASCAR wrecking?

scene.alt: Side-by-side diagram showing a controlled bump vs a hard crash.

choices.label: No, some contact is part of hard racing.
Yes, any contact is a wreck.

explanation.correct: Right. A bump or controlled contact while passing is racing. A wreck is reckless contact that destroys a car or ends a race.
explanation.incorrect: Contact happens in close racing. A bump to move someone, a slight tap to get by or defensive contact is racing. A wreck is when someone loses control, crashes into the wall or a car is heavily damaged.

options.text: The contact was aggressive but within the bounds of acceptable racing.
The car broke down due to engine trouble.
The pit crew worked very hard during the stop.

payload.translation: The bump or contact was aggressive but not malicious; it is part of the sport.

followUps.line: Hard racing includes bumps, tight passes and defensive moves that do not ruin a car.
followUps.why: Drivers accept some contact as the cost of trying to pass or defend position.

followUps.line: Wrecking is when the contact is reckless, intentional or ends in a crash; fans and drivers draw that line.
followUps.why: The culture polices itself: wreck someone and payback or a bad reputation follow.

payload.prompt: Match the contact type to what it is.

pairs.definition: Hard but acceptable contact: bumps, blocks and tight passes within the bounds of the sport.
Reckless or intentional contact that destroys a car, ends a race or is clearly over the line.
Deliberately crashing another driver, which is penalized by NASCAR and draws fines, suspensions or payback.

distractorDefinitions: Losing grip and sliding off the track.
Changing lanes slowly on the straightaway.

explanation.summary: Racing and wrecking are separated by intent and outcome. A bump is racing; a hard crash is wrecking.

payload.prompt: He moved down, you moved down, and you both slid. Racing or wrecking?

facts.label: The move
facts.value: You tried to pass low, he defended, both cars slid

facts.label: Result
facts.value: Both cars are okay; you lost the pass but no damage

facts.label: Your speed
facts.value: You were committed to the pass

facts.label: His move
facts.value: He moved down to defend his line

options.label: That was racing.
options.consequence: You accepted the risk and so did he. No one wrecked; it was a clean battle.
considerations: No one went over the top.

options.label: He wrecked you.
options.consequence: He defended his line; that is not wrecking. If you want to complain to NASCAR, they will laugh.
considerations: Both sliding is part of the game.

payload.expertNote: Racing means everyone knows the risk. If you commit to a pass and the other driver defends, slides happen and that is racing.
